To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
HIV-specific antibodies produced by the intestinal mucosal immune system of HIV-exposed babies are capable to inhibit HIV infection of human cells in vitro.

HIV-specific antibodies, derived from B cell immunity of the intestinal mucosa of breastfed children exposed to HIV-1, are produced and excreted in their stools, and that these antibodies possess major functional properties against the virus.

HIV-specific B cell-derived immune defense of the gastrointestinal tract is activated to produce antibodies in children exposed to HIV-1 via breast-feeding, and that these antibodies harbour functional properties against HIV-1.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of mucosal immune response to HIV in children exposed to HIV via breastfeeding.

the following objectives: 1. to evaluate whether the intestinal mucosa of infants exposed to HIV via breastfeeding can be activated to produce HIV antibodies, 2. to characterize the HIV-specific antibodies produced by the intestinal mucosal immune system in HIV-exposed children.
the development of a prophylaxis vaccine against HIV in breast-fed children.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the intestinal mucosa of HIV-exposed babies produces HIV-specific antibodies, and that these antibodies harbour in vitro major functional capacities against HIV.

the intestinal mucosa of HIV-exposed infants is capable of producing HIV-specific antibodies with in vitro anti-HIV activity, but this does not necessarily mean that these antibodies are protective against HIV infection in vivo.

HIV-specific antibodies in breast milk and stools of children continuously exposed to the HIV via breast- feeding are derived from the B cells of the intestinal mucosa, and are able to inhibit the attachment and the infection of the intestinal mucosal epithelial cells and macrophages by HIV.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have demonstrated that the mucosal immune system is activated and produces antibodies against HIV in children exposed to HIV via breastfeeding.
the intestinal mucosa of HIV-exposed infants produces antibodies with functional properties against HIV, and that these antibodies may represent an effective immune defense of the gastro-intestine.

the intestinal mucosa of breastfed children exposed to HIV-1 by their HIV-1 infected mothers produces HIV-specific antibodies with major functional properties against R5- and/or X4- tropism HIV-1 strains.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the intestinal mucosa of HIV-exposed infants is able to generate HIV-specific antibodies with major functional properties against infection.
the intestinal mucosa of breastfed children exposed to HIV is able to produce HIV-specific IgA and IgA, which are capable to inhibit attachment and infection of HIV to the intestinal epithelium.
breast milk and stools of children exposed to breast milk HIV are rich in HIV-specific antibodies, which may protect the children against infection by HIV-1.
